html:
Most design decisions come down to one question: is this fast enough, and does it fit? You can't answer it without a feel for how long things take and how much data moves. This guide gives you that feel, and a way to estimate a system's size in two minutes.

Latency vs Throughput

  • Latency is how long one thing takes: a request answered in 80 ms.
  • Throughput is how many things get done per second: 5,000 requests per second.

They are related but different. A highway has the same travel time (latency) with one lane or six, but six lanes carry more cars (throughput). Adding servers usually raises throughput; making one request faster needs less work per request, a cache, or a shorter distance.

The Numbers

Exact values depend on the hardware, so remember the orders of magnitude, not the digits:

Operation Roughly
Read from CPU cache 1 ns
Read from main memory (RAM) 100 ns
Read 1 MB sequentially from memory 10 µs
Random read from an SSD 20–100 µs
Round trip inside one data center 0.5 ms
Read 1 MB sequentially from an SSD 0.5–1 ms
Disk seek on a spinning hard drive 5–10 ms
Round trip between continents 100–150 ms

What they tell you:

  • Memory is about 1,000 times faster than an SSD, and an SSD is much faster than a network call to another continent. That's why caches live in memory.
  • A call inside the data center costs about half a millisecond. A page that makes 50 sequential calls to other services spends 25 ms just waiting, before any work.
  • Distance is physics. Light in fiber needs about 70 ms to cross the Atlantic and back. Only moving the data closer, with a CDN or a second region, makes that faster.

Percentiles, Not Averages

An average hides the slow requests. Measure percentiles instead:

  • p50 (median): half the requests are faster.
  • p99: 99% are faster, 1% are slower.

If one page calls 100 backends in parallel, it waits for the slowest one, so almost every page view hits some backend's p99. That's why big systems care about tail latency, and why "fast on average" isn't enough.

Back-of-the-Envelope Estimates

Before designing anything, estimate the load. Round hard: you want the order of magnitude.

Useful shortcuts:

  • A day has about 100,000 seconds (86,400).
  • 1 request per second is about 100,000 a day, and 2.5 million a month.
  • Peak traffic is often 2 to 3 times the average.

Example: A Photo-Sharing App

Say 10 million users are active daily, each views 50 photos and uploads 1 photo a day.

  • Reads: 10 M × 50 = 500 M views a day ÷ 100,000 s = 5,000 reads per second, about 15,000 at peak.
  • Writes: 10 M uploads a day = 100 writes per second. A read-heavy system: caching will matter more than write speed.
  • Storage: 10 M photos × 500 KB = 5 TB a day, about 1.8 PB a year. That's object storage, not a database column.
  • Bandwidth: 5,000 views/s × 500 KB = 2.5 GB/s out. A CDN has to serve most of it.

Four lines of math, and you already know the design needs a CDN, object storage and caches.

Common Mistakes

  • Ignoring peaks. Systems fall over at the Monday 9 a.m. spike, not at the daily average.
  • Mixing bits and bytes. Network speeds are in bits: a 1 Gbit/s link moves about 125 MB/s.
  • Forgetting replication. Three copies of the data triple the storage.
  • Being too precise. "About 5,000 per second" is the right answer; "5,787" wastes interview time.

The Answer in Short

  1. Latency is the time for one operation; throughput is how many per second.
  2. Memory is nanoseconds, SSDs are microseconds, networks are milliseconds, other continents are about 100 ms.
  3. Measure p99, not averages: users feel the slow tail.
  4. Estimate with round numbers: 100,000 seconds a day, peaks 2–3× the average.
  5. Let the estimate drive the design: reads vs writes, storage size and bandwidth.
